> [Q1]: How does your analysis extend beyond linear models?
> 

Thanks for this question! We are actively thinking of solvable nonlinear settings like random feature model, feature regression / kernel regression with structured feature or kernel. Where we have relatively clean expressions of the learned denoiser or score model. 

For example, for feature regression case $\mathbf D(\mathbf x,\sigma)=W_\sigma\Phi(\mathbf x+\sigma \mathbf z,\sigma)+b_\sigma$, the denoiser loss reads, 
$$
\mathcal L_\sigma=\mathbb E_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z} \|W_\sigma\Phi(\mathbf x+\sigma \mathbf z,\sigma)+b_\sigma-\mathbf x\|^2
$$
This is still a general least square problem. We can still express the weights through feature covariance matrix and cross covariance with $\mathbf x$. 
$$
W_\sigma^\star
= \Sigma_{x\phi} \, \Sigma_{\phi\phi}^{-1}
$$
$$
b_\sigma^\star
= \mu_x - W_\sigma^\star \,\mu_\phi
$$
$$
\Sigma_{x\phi}
\;\equiv\;
\mathbb E_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z}
\big[\mathbf x\ \Phi^\top(\mathbf x+\sigma \mathbf z,\sigma)\big]-\mu_x\mu_\phi^\top
$$
$$
\Sigma_{\phi\phi}
\;\equiv\;
\mathbb E_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z}
\big[\Phi(\mathbf x+\sigma \mathbf z,\sigma)\Phi^\top(\mathbf x+\sigma \mathbf z,\sigma)\big]-\mu_\phi\mu_\phi^\top.
$$
One can see structures in it, and use random matrix like technique to derive the variance of the learned denoiser or score. Some previous works have made progress applying RMT to the random feature case, [3] [4]. 

The foreseeable difficulty lies in solving PF-ODE, i.e. the generating map itself. Generally, it will not have a close form solution like in our linear case. So one will need other method to analyze the covariance of the solution due to dataset realization. One possible route is through **sensitivity analysis of (PF-)ODE**, i.e. linearize the dependency of ODE solution on parameter, i.e. the summary statistics of data (e.g. mean and covariance in linear case). 

$$
\mathbf x(\sigma;\Theta)\approx \mathbf x(\sigma;\bar\Theta) + \frac{\partial\mathbf{x}(\sigma;\Theta)}{\partial\Theta}(\Theta-\bar \Theta)
$$

Then one can propagate the variance of summary statistics to variance of score / denoiser vector field and the variance of generated samples. 

The full treatment of the nonlinear, feature regression case would need further development. We expect to explore these nonlinear settings in follow-up work.

[1] Li, Xiang, Yixiang Dai, and Qing Qu. "Understanding generalizability of diffusion models requires rethinking the hidden gaussian structure." Advances in neural information processing systems 37 (2024): 57499-57538.

[2] Wang, B., & Vastola, J. J. (2024). The unreasonable effectiveness of gaussian score approximation for diffusion models and its applications. TMLR

[3] Bonnaire, T., Urfin, R., Biroli, G., & Mézard, M. (2025). Why Diffusion Models Don't Memorize: The Role of Implicit Dynamical Regularization in Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17638 

[4] George, A. J., Veiga, R., & Macris, N. (2025). Denoising score matching with random features: Insights on diffusion models from precise learning curves. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00336

$$

$$
$$
b_\sigma^\star

$$
$$

$$

$$

So one will need other method to analyze the covariance of the solution due to dataset realization. One possible route is through **sensitivity analysis of ODE**, i.e. linearize the dependency of ODE solution on parameter, i.e. the summary statistics of data (e.g. mean and covariance in linear case). 
$$

Then one can propagate the variance of summary statistics to variance of score / denoiser vector field and the variance of generated samples. 

The full treatment of the nonlinear, feature regression case would need further development. We expect to explore these nonlinear settings in follow-up work.

### **Q2: Sensitivity to non-Gaussian, structured datasets**

Great question. Natural images are known to be strongly non-Gaussian, yet the linear theory predicts global structure surprisingly well.

**Theory:** At high noise, any accurate learned score must be nearly linear, and deep models prefer smoother vector fields (simplicity bias). Since high-noise sampling determines coarse layout, the linear predictor accurately captures low-frequency structure [3,4].

**Empirics:** To stress-test this, we conducted extensive UNet training experiments on **five more diverse datasets across dataset scales**:
- CIFAR-100
- LSUN bedroom (32px, 64px)
- LSUN church (32px, 64px)

Total: **60+ additional training runs**.
We generated both **visual** and **quantitative** results analogous to Figures 1 and 5. We now include **dozens** of new figures. Highlights:

- Generated samples from both splits are **closer to the consistent linear predictor than to nearest neighbors in their own training splits**, even in highly multimodal settings (CIFAR10).
    - **Only one** CIFAR-100 split shows linear and NN baselines comparable—matching the reviewer’s intuition about extreme multimodality.
- The **quantitative consistency** between RMT prediction and UNet / DiT sampling remains robust.
- We also newly show (Fig. 32) that **as $n$ increases,** for a fixed noise seed, **DNN generations converge toward the linear prediction** — supporting the linear predictor as a high-data-limit solution.

Across datasets we consistently observe RMT-predicted effects: Overshrinkage; Spectral-wise stronger alignment in top eigen-modes; Seed-wise prediction of inhomogeneity of reproducibility (see Figs. 26–30, 34–41, 37–48)

We will consolidate these extended results into clearer summary figures for the final version.

References
[0]: Wang, B., & Vastola, J. J. (2024). The unreasonable effectiveness of gaussian score approximation for diffusion models and its applications, TMLR. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09726
[1] Bonnaire, T., Urfin, R., Biroli, G., & Mézard, M. (2025). Why Diffusion Models Don't Memorize: The Role of Implicit Dynamical Regularization in Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17638
[2] George, A. J., Veiga, R., & Macris, N. (2025). Denoising score matching with random features: Insights on diffusion models from precise learning curves. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00336
[3] Wang, B., & Vastola, J. J. (2023). Diffusion models generate images like painters: an analytical theory of outline first, details later.  https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.02490
[4] Spectral autoregression. https://sander.ai/2024/09/02/spectral-autoregression.html

Thanks for your rebuttal. I will list my remaining questions below:

(1) I agree the the consistency / concentration of some “summary statistics” across dataset splits could be the answer, but this paper only studies linear features, hence the contribution is kind of limited. Can any results of your work guide us to further study what contributes to the consistency beyond linear features?

(2) Can you better explain how your work can help design test time scaling algorithms? Can you provide some concrete example to show good noise should avoid disagreement between data splits?

title.value: Rebuttal to Reviewer 7EKG: Experiments on Additional Datasets (CIFAR100, LSUN bedroom, church 32 and 64), consistent results.

comment.value:
We sincerely thank Reviewer `7EKG` for their careful reading and constructive comments on our submission, especially for noting that our results *“yield novel and non-trivial theoretical contributions”* and that the *“contribution to linear theory alone could be substantial enough to approve acceptance.”*

The reviewer’s major concern is that the datasets used to validate the theory were too homogeneous. We fully agree this was an important limitation of the original submission. Below we summarize the additional experiments and clarifications we performed in response, and hope these results demonstrate that **our findings are not cherry-picked** but instead **robust across diverse datasets**.

---

### **[W1, W2] Dataset Diversity and Homogeneity Concern**

We agree with the reviewer that face datasets are particularly structured; as noted, even their first moment (mean image) contains perceptual information (e.g., the classic Eigenfaces work [R2]). We appreciate the reviewer pointing this out.

To directly address the homogeneity concern, we expanded our experimental suite beyond face datasets. We trained CNN-UNet models across varying split sizes on the following additional datasets commonly used in generative modeling:

- **CIFAR-100** (32 px)
- **LSUN_church** (32 px and 64 px)
- **LSUN_bedroom** (32 px and 64 px)

These datasets contain large pose variation, diverse scene layouts, and multimodal category structure, making them significantly less homogeneous than facial datasets.

**We welcome further dataset suggestions from the reviewer.**

We generated both **visual** and **quantitative** results analogous to Figures 1 and 5 in the main paper. Numerous new visual comparisons (Fig. 7–20) are now included in Appendix B.1. Although the linear-theory predictions are not always perceptually perfect, the **quantitative agreement (especially MSE)** remains strong across datasets.

Crucially, the core motivating observation—

**generated samples across splits are consistently closer to the linear predictor than to the nearest-neighbor from the training set**—

holds across all new datasets, including the multimodal **CIFAR-10** case (new Figs. 7 and 13).

The only exception is one split of **CIFAR-100**, where the linear and NN baselines are comparable—suggesting that the linear approximation can break down in extremely multimodal regimes.

One additional evidence suggesting the relevance of the Gaussian linear solution is in the new Fig.32, which shows, with increasing training dataset sizes (n), the generated sample of deep network from a fixed initial seed gradually approach the generated sample from linear theory with the same initial seed. Showing the Gaussian linear predictor is related to the high data limit of deep network. 

Across datasets we also consistently observed effects predicted by RMT: overshrinkage, stronger alignment in top eigen-modes, and accurate prediction of which initial seeds yield consistent reconstructions. Quantitative evidence is given in Figs. 26–30, 34–48, and 37–41.

For rebuttal clarity we present the full set of extended results; in the final camera-ready version we will condense these into more compact figures in the style of Figure 5.

> Q1. Since is a $\kappa(\sigma^2)$ key identity in the paper, I think it would be better to present it explicitly in the text rather only in the Appendix.
> 

We totally agree! **Could the reviewer clarify which identity would be useful to be put in main text**? Currently, we have included the Silverstein self-consistent equation (Eq. 5), the one point deterministic equivalence for resolvent (Eq. 4), but left the two point DE case in the appendix. 

> Q2. In line 255, what is the definition of $S_D(x)$?
> 

The definition is just the full covariance matrix ($d\times d$) of the denoiser $\mathbf D$ due the realization of empirical covariance $\hat \Sigma$. 

$$Var_{\hat{\Sigma}}(\mathbf {D_{\hat{\Sigma}}}(\mathbf x,\sigma))$$

> Q3. Could you provide results on datasets with more diverse classes of data, and visual samples from models trained on such datasets. As I mentioned above, an assessment of sample quality would be crucial (using e.g. FID or similar score).
> 

Now we included extensive visual examples from `CIFAR10`, `CIFAR100`, `LSUNbedroom` and `LSUNchurch` 32 and 64 pixel; `FFHQ` 32 and 64 pixel, and the corresponding distance quantification in appendix B.1. 

> Q4.Specifically, please provide visual results (similar to Fig.1 and 5) for CIFAR experiment.

We made the new experiments on CIFAR100 and included the visual results for both CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. 

> Q5. Also, state how many classes of the CIFAR datatset were used in the experiment.

In the original experiment, we used `CIFAR10`. In the new experiments, we also used `CIFAR100` to show that our results generalize to highly “multi-modal” datasets. 

> Q6. minor/typos: l.438: double 'linear’

Thanks for mentioning, we fixed the typo in the updated version.

summary.value: This paper studies the surprising consistency of diffusion models trained on different, non-overlapping subsets of the same dataset: even when trained on distinct splits, models produce very similar outputs for the same noise seed. The authors trace this phenomenon to a linear Gaussian effect, showing that much of the generated signal can already be explained by the shared dataset statistics. To formalize this intuition, the paper develops a Random Matrix Theory (RMT) framework for linear diffusion models, quantifying how finite dataset size affects both the expectation and variance of learned denoisers and sampling maps. Key mechanisms include renormalization of noise scale, variance decomposition, and full trajectory analysis. Finally, the paper validates these RMT predictions empirically on UNet and DiT architectures, confirming that the same principles explain inhomogeneous consistency across data splits even beyond the linear regime.

strengths.value:
**1.Principled theoretical framework using RMT:** The paper provides a rigorous Random Matrix Theory (RMT) framework to analyze the consistency of diffusion models across different data splits. By quantifying both the expectation and variance of linear denoisers under finite-sample effects, it offers clear insights into how dataset statistics and sample size shape generative outputs, establishing a strong theoretical baseline for understanding cross-split reproducibility.

**2. Empirical validation on diffusion models:** Despite focusing on linear theory, the paper demonstrates that its predictions hold qualitatively for practical deep models, including UNet and DiT architectures. The validation highlights phenomena such as overshrinkage of low-variance modes, anisotropy across eigenmodes, and inhomogeneity across inputs, bridging the gap between theory and practice and providing actionable insights for understanding model stability.

weaknesses.value:
**1. Only focus on the linear denoiser.** The theoretical analysis in the paper is primarily restricted to linear denoisers, which makes the mathematical derivations tractable via Random Matrix Theory. While this provides valuable insight into the role of dataset statistics and finite-sample effects, it does not fully capture the behavior of real-world diffusion models, which are highly nonlinear and overparameterized (e.g., UNet and DiT architectures). As a result, the direct applicability of the theoretical results to practical settings is limited.

**2. Inconsistent notation:** In several places, the manuscript uses inconsistent formatting for mathematical symbols, which can confuse readers about whether a symbol represents a scalar, vector, or matrix. For example, in Lines 132–136, the population mean $\mu$ and $\hat{\mu}$ are written in plain font. Typically, vectors and matrices are written in boldface to distinguish them from scalars in the paper. The inconsistency makes it harder to follow derivations and can lead to ambiguity, especially in formulas involving differences between the population and empirical quantities.

questions.value:
**Q1.** The theoretical framework focuses on linear denoisers, but most practical diffusion models are highly nonlinear. How well do the RMT predictions quantitatively carry over to nonlinear architectures like UNet or DiT? Could the authors provide insights or bounds on when the linear approximation breaks down, or suggest extensions of their framework to account for nonlinearity?

**Q2.** The analysis assumes Gaussian-like statistics in the data. How sensitive are the predictions to deviations from this assumption, such as strongly non-Gaussian or structured datasets (e.g., natural images with heavy tails, multimodality, or complex correlations)?

summary.value: This paper addresses consistency in diffusion models through the lens of random matrix theory. The observation under study is that diffusion models trained on disjoint splits of the dataset produce outputs with similar results for the same input noise. The authors suggest that this arises from shared Gaussian statistics in the sub-datasets. The authors make use of a linear denoiser, and proceed to show what effects beyond Gaussian statisstics can be learned from random matrix theory and demonstrate that linear denoisers on varying dataset sizes share a combination of renormalization, anisotropy, and inhomogeneity. The authors conclude by pointing out some of these effects in trained diffusion models

strengths.value:
- I think this is a really interesting way to analyze diffusion and a fascinating phenomenon that I have not heard a good answer to. I am excited to see work that tries to address these questions in this way
- While the theory relies on a very strong assumption (see also weaknesses), I thoroughly enjoyed the depth with which the authors explored the topics.
- Interpretations are given throughout the paper to help the reader understand the math.

weaknesses.value:
- While the authors have done a great job in presenting the work, its complexity still makes this a difficult paper to follow, since a lot of concepts are uncommon in diffusion models. I understand this is a difficult topic to write about, and the authors have done quite a good job, but I do still think the high bar of entry of this paper is overall a weakness.
- In general, the results seem to be very dependent on the linear denoiser assumption. The authors do make an effort to include experiments and give broader interpretations, but the bulk of the work remains focused on this narrow setting.
- There are a few grammar errors floating around in the text, these would be easily captured with a pass trough a language model.

questions.value:
- In the motivating example, the authors suggest that because the only thing the linear model captures are Gaussian statistics, and that because the two linear model results give the same, and are also similar to the DiT and Unet outputs, similarity arises because of shared Gaussian statistics. It would be great to see a more direct proof of this assertion, which could quite easily be done by reducing the dataset into smaller and smaller chunks until the Gaussian statistics start to differ. This should coincide with a change in visual features if the authors hypothesis is correct. Have the authors considered such an experiment?
- It seems as if the similarity in the rightmost column in Fig 5A is much less pronounced than in Fig 1A., while to the best of what I can find out these experiments should match. Can the authors comment?

summary.value: This work studies the consistency phenomenon observed in diffusion models, that is, trained models on nonoverlapping data splits learn similar noise-to-image mappings. They observe same consistency phenomenon occurs in the linear diffusion model, which is fully characterized by mean and covariance of the underlying data distribution. With the help of random matrix theory, the authors characterize the variance of empirical linear diffusion models compared to the population one, discovering the 'shrinkage along eigen mode' effects. Several predictions based on the theory are made.

strengths.value:
1. The analysis is rigorous and valid, accurately predicting the behaviors of linear models.

2. The discussion about "magic" noise is interesting and can inspire further research.

weaknesses.value:
1. Previous work [1] has already attributed the consistency of diffusion models to the similarity of empirical covariances among data splits. This work sharpens this argument with rigorous analysis, but is still limited to the linear case. It remains unknown what else besides linear structures contribute to the observed consistency. 

2. Similar to the first point, the key theoretical results that characterize the variance caused by the empirical splits may not extend beyond linear model.

3. It is unclear how the theory in this paper can guide us design better diffusion models.

[1] Li, Xiang, Yixiang Dai, and Qing Qu. "Understanding generalizability of diffusion models requires rethinking the hidden gaussian structure." Advances in neural information processing systems 37 (2024): 57499-57538.

questions.value:
1. How does your analysis extend beyond linear models?

2. It is mentioned in discussion, 'magic noise' should not be aligned with directions that disagree among data splits. Why this is the case? Is it possible that although the directions do not align across data splits, they still capture meaningful structure of the data and making the initial noise align with them can produce high quality images? What properties do you think a good initial noise should have such that the generated samples have higher quality?

summary.value: The paper studies the consistency of linear (Gaussian) denoisers across distinct training datasets, that is: how close will be samples generated using the same latent seed by the different models. The analysis is done through the lens of spectral theory of Bach (2024), where denoisers are treated as operators acting on the sample space. It is shown that the expected denoiser converges to the true denoiser in some weak sense (where both dimension and number of samples tend to $\infty$), where noise scale is re-noarmalized to absorb random fluctuations, regardless of the training data split. The conclusion is that linear components with small eigenvalues are pulled towards the true data mean. The *variance* of this desnoiser is decomposed into an "anisotropic" component depending on the eigenvector direction and an "inhomogeneous" part depending on initial sample deviation from center. It is then claimed that deep diffusion models exhibit the same behavior: as number of samples grows, models trained on distinct split of the training set produce similar samples.

strengths.value:
1. The presentation is sufficient for a rather technical subject. Presenting results for "one-step" denoisers (Sec. 4) is an easy to follow introduction to the results in Sec. 5 for the Wiener filter.

2. The results for linear regressors (Sec.4) although adopted from Bach(2024) seems to yield novel and non-trivial theoretical contributions (Propostions 1 and 2). 

3. The results in Sec 5. are novel as well.

weaknesses.value:
Overall, I think that the contribution to linear theory alone could be substantial enough to approve acceptance. However, I find the general claims about diffusion models (starting with the title), arguably, not convincing enough. More specifically:

1. Starting with  the "MOTIVATING EMPIRICAL OBSERVATION" part, (Sec.3, Fig.1) is not quite a good case in my opinion for the following reasons: (A) The authors claim that "Strikingly, the linear Gaussian predictor ... already accounts for much of this behavior" (l.159). I disagree about how *striking* this outcome is. Linear models such as PCA, ICA or Factor analysis  [R1, Sec. 12.2.4] are used for decades for generating samples from a low-dimensional latent space. This is especially true for structured data such as face images [R2]. It is no wonder then that on such a dataset general solutions will act similar to linear ones. Thus, a demonstration on "faces" dataset is not a sufficient test case. (B) Even on faces data, `linear' theory does not always produce quality samples as can be seen on Fig. 5.  (C) I suspect that for less structured data (such as natural images) a demonstration similar to Fig.1 could not work.

2. The same concern applies to "VALIDATING PREDICTIONS ON DEEP NETWORKS" (Sec.6): (A) Three of the demonstrated datasets consist again of face images. (B) On the CIFAR dataset (10 or 100 classes? authors do not specify...), the authors do not present the visual overcomes of models (deep or linear) which are crucial in order to asses the trained models quality. Whenever the model fails to catch the data distribution, consistency can be an an undesirable feature. For one (trivial) example, a model producing 0-images is very consistent but at the expanse of low-quality samples. (C) overall, it seems that the presented visual results are cherry-picked.

If the above weaknesses could be adequately addressed I will be happy to raise the score and recommend acceptance. 


[R1] Christopher M Bishop and Nasser M Nasrabadi. Pattern recognition and machine learning,
volume 4. Springer, 2006.

[R2] Turk, Matthew, and Alex Pentland. "Eigenfaces for recognition." Journal of cognitive neuroscience 3.1 (1991): 71-86.

title.value: Submission Desk Rejected by Program Chairs

comment.value:
Sorry for the delayed response!

We sincerely thank reviewer qP44 for their careful evaluation of our work and for the encouraging comments. We are glad the reviewer finds this to be “*a really interesting way to analyze diffusion and a fascinating phenomenon that I have not heard a good answer to*,” and that we have “*done a great job in presenting the work*.”

### **[W1]— High barrier of entry**

We appreciate the reviewer’s understanding.

Indeed, the mathematical tools employed here (random matrix theory) are not yet widely used in the diffusion modeling community, despite their prevalence in deep learning and regression theory. As authors, we were also impressed by how naturally and powerfully these tools apply to diffusion models — especially under the linear denoiser formulation. We hope this work can serve as a bridge:

- inviting diffusion researchers to engage with RMT-based techniques, and
- highlighting to RMT/learning theory researchers a compelling new application domain.


### **[W2] — Dependence on linear denoiser assumption**

We acknowledge this limitation and thank the reviewer for the fair assessment.

The linear denoiser case is analytically the cleanest, enabling closed-form and highly interpretable results. However, our framework naturally extends to structured and random feature regression, where the optimal denoiser also admits closed-form characterization:

$$
\mathbf D(\mathbf x,\sigma)=W_\sigma\Phi(\mathbf x+\sigma \mathbf z,\sigma)+b_\sigma
$$

$$
W_\sigma^\star
= \Sigma_{x\phi} \, \Sigma_{\phi\phi}^{-1}\quad,\quad
b_\sigma^\star
= \mu_x - W_\sigma^\star \,\mu_\phi
$$

$$
\Sigma_{x\phi}
\;\equiv\;
\mathbb E_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z}
\big[\mathbf x\ \Phi^\top(\mathbf x+\sigma \mathbf z,\sigma)\big]-\mu_x\mu_\phi^\top
$$

$$
\Sigma_{\phi\phi}
\;\equiv\;
\mathbb E_{\mathbf x,\mathbf z}
\big[\Phi(\mathbf x+\sigma \mathbf z,\sigma)\Phi^\top(\mathbf x+\sigma \mathbf z,\sigma)\big]-\mu_\phi\mu_\phi^\top
$$

In such cases, random matrix theory can again quantify the variability of the denoiser across dataset realizations. For the generative trajectory, the PFODE no longer has a closed-form solution, but we may apply ODE sensitivity analysis:

$$
\mathbf x(\sigma;\Theta)\approx \mathbf x(\sigma;\bar\Theta) + \frac{\partial\mathbf{x}(\sigma;\Theta)}{\partial\Theta}(\Theta-\bar \Theta)
$$

We see this as a promising path toward understanding generalization beyond the linear setting and are actively working on it.

### **[W3]— Grammar issues**

Thank you for the suggestion. We will perform a thorough proofreading pass (including use of a language model) to correct remaining grammar errors.

### **[Q1]— Direct test of the Gaussian-statistics hypothesis**

We appreciate this insightful suggestion.

Figure 5A implements a version of this idea: reducing dataset size changes empirical Gaussian statistics, and we observe that:

- linear-theory samples remain relatively similar across splits, while
- DNN-based samples increasingly **memorize** training samples (e.g., at n=300,1000) and diverge from each other.

We think this divergence is expected: in the memorization regime, DNN are not well approximated by linear denoiser, so the predictive power of theory degrades. In general, the linear solution will be **more consistent** than deep networks and doesn’t capture the memorization behavior. 

However, we are conducting another variant of this experiment, i.e. 

- sorting data along some PC or certain feature,
- splitting dataset not randomly but by the sorted feature value.
- then even with higher $n$, this will make the mean and / or covariance of the two splits differ.
- then train diffusion models on the two sorted splits.

Based on our theory, we expect the generated samples from the two splits to diverge more under such systematic statistics shifts. These new experiments are underway and will be included in our revision. We apologize for the timing.
While my comments and questions are perhaps minor, I would greatly appreciate it if the authors could nonetheless address them too, or refer me to relevant other parts of the rebuttal.

### **[Q2] — Visual discrepancy between FFHQ32 (Fig.1A) and FFHQ64 (Fig.5A)**

Thank you for noticing this.

The two figures indeed correspond to different resolutions (32px vs. 64px). At higher resolution (FFHQ64), the linear denoiser appears less visually compelling. Nonetheless, the **quantitative** result remains strong:

- linear-theory samples are **closer to each other** than to the nearest training examples across splits (see Fig. 6 for distance matrices and Fig. 16 for additional visual samples)

This pattern is also observed in prior work — linear models degrade at larger image scales (e.g. CelebA 256px in [1] Fig. 4 & 13).

Our interpretation is that:

> at low noise scales/high frequencies, image statistics deviate strongly from Gaussian, requiring a richer score model.

Recent progress using **local score machines** (patch-wise softmax/delta mixtures) supports this direction and likely a better model of low noise regime [2,3].


### **References**

[1] Wang & Vastola (2023). *Diffusion models generate images like painters: an analytical theory of outline first, details later.*

[2] Niedoba et al. (2024). *Towards a mechanistic explanation of diffusion model generalization.*

[3] Kamb & Ganguli (2024). *An analytic theory of creativity in convolutional diffusion models.*

title.value: Global Response and Summary of Revisions

comment.value:
### Global Response and Summary of Revisions

We are grateful for all the reviewers for their thoughtful feedback of our paper and unanimously positive evaluation of our theory. In response, we have substantially strengthened the submission along several dimensions—particularly by expanding the empirical validations—to provide greater confidence in our conclusions.

**Expanded empirical validation.**

To address reviewer concerns about dataset diversity and applicability to non Gaussian data, we performed more than 60 additional UNet training runs on five new datasets (CIFAR-100; LSUN bedroom and LSUN church at 32px and 64px). These experiments directly examine the robustness of our theoretical predictions in more realistic and highly multimodal settings.

**Strengthened visual and quantitative results.**

We added extensive new analyses paralleling Figures 1 and 5 of the main paper, with dozens of new figures added. Across all datasets, at non-memorizing regime, generated samples from different splits remain closer to the linear-theory predictions than to nearest neighbors in their respective training data (with one outlier in the highly multi-modal regime) (Appendix B.1, Fig. 7–20). Further, as dataset scale $n$ increases, generated sample from DNN approach the linear theory predicted outcome with the matching initial seed (Fig.32). We also consistently observe the RMT-predicted effects, including overshrinkage, dominant spectral-mode alignment, and seed-wise inhomogeneous reproducibility (see Figs. 26–30, 34–41, 37–48).

**Improved clarity and presentation.**

### **(1) Beyond linear features: what contributes to consistency?**

We fully agree with the reviewer that consistency across dataset splits may ultimately depend on **higher-order** structure beyond linear / Gaussian features. In this paper, we restricted our analysis to the linear regime and its associated Gaussian statistics—not because these are exhaustive, but because they provide the cleanest theoretical foundation.

To study structure beyond linear features, one needs to systematically vary the **feature class** used to approximate the score function $\Phi(x+\sigma z, \sigma)$. Different function classes correspond to different implicit **energy functions** and thus different “summary statistics” of the data:

| **Model class** | **Captured statistics** |
| --- | --- |
| Linear | Global Gaussian |
| Linear convolutions | Patch-level Gaussian |
| Linear + nonlinear | Exponential-family extensions |
| Local score machines [5] | Non-Gaussian local statistics |

A systematic comparison across these classes would directly address what statistics drive split consistency **beyond** the linear regime—a very interesting direction that we highlight for future work.

### **(2) How do our results guide test-time scaling?**

Diffusion sampling begins from noise in the **data space**, so it is informative to analyze that noise in the **data covariance eigenframe**. For the linear PFODE score solution (Eq. 3), we have:

$$
x_{\hat\Sigma}(x_{\sigma_T},0)=\mu+\sum_{k}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{k}+\sigma_T^2}}
\mathbf{u}\_k\mathbf{u}\_k^{\top}(x_{\sigma_T}-\mu)
$$

Thus the amplification/shrinkage of initial noise along eigenmode k is:

$$
\underbrace{
\sigma_T\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{k}+\sigma_T^2}}
}_{\text{amplification factor}}
$$

- **Top-eigen directions** ($\lambda_k$  large) are **strongly amplified**
- **Low-eigen directions** are **contracted / denoised away**

This leads to a key insight:

> If the initial noise has too much power in the top eigenspace, those components will be amplified rather than denoised
> 

Our new visual results (Fig. 49–51) demonstrate exactly this:

- Amplifying noise along top eigenvectors produces **consistent structured distortions**
- Suppressing it yields **cleaner and more reproducible samples**
- Perturbations confined to low-eigen directions are **nearly invisible**

In addition, our RMT analysis shows that **across-split variability** is dominated by these high-eigen directions. Therefore:

> A good test-time noise policy should avoid injecting too much power into directions that both amplify quickly and vary across dataset splits.
> 

This reframes resampling/perturbing noise in test-time scaling:

- Consider **anisotropic** noise structure
- Avoid directions that exhibit **high amplification + high variability**

Reproducibility is one consequence—but the underlying principle is likely the **anisotropic structure of noise space and the contraction and expansion dynamics** of the generative map.

### **W1: Only focusing on the linear denoiser**

We agree that this paper focuses on the linear denoiser. Our goal is to develop random matrix theory tools in the simplest possible setting where they can yield clean and interpretable progress.

However, this simplified model can still shed light on realistic diffusion architectures for principled theoretical reasons. Per previous results [0], the linear denoiser is a good approximation of neural network denoisers for many noise scales (especially high noise). Thus, even trained nonlinear diffusion models (UNet, DiT) exhibit linear-like behavior in that regime. Since sampling at high noise determines global structure in generated samples, linear theory still yields meaningful predictions about nonlinear models.

### **Q1: Predictive power and limits of RMT for nonlinear models**

> “How well do the RMT predictions quantitatively carry over to nonlinear architectures like UNet or DiT?”
> 

A key prediction that carries over robustly is the **inhomogeneous effect of the initial noise seed**.

Using only the population mean and covariance, we can predict which initial noise seeds yield consistent generations across data splits and which do not. Across models and datasets, the predicted consistency correlates strongly with measured MSE (Pearson ~0.3–0.5). We are not aware of alternative techniques capable of such predictions without RMT.

We also observe that the differences between UNet/DiT denoisers across splits show the same **spectral** and **spatial** structure that RMT predicts.

> “Insights or bounds on when the linear approximation breaks down?”
> 

There are two key regimes where linear approx. breakdown :

- **Dataset size** $n$ — When data are too few, linear function approximator cannot memorize more than one data point; nonlinear denoisers are required (Fig. 5A). The exact transition data scale depends on architecture and dataset structure and remains an active area of research (e.g. recent work [1]).
- **Noise level** $\sigma$ — At low noise, linear approximation fails. Theory guranttees linearity should hold when $\sigma^2 \gg \lambda_1$ (top PCA variance) [0]. Empirically, linearity holds even for smaller noise scale, likely due to **simplicity bias** of deep networks toward smoother vector fields.

Nonlinear behavior is important and highly worthy of further theoretical development.
